lesson.title: React useEffect() Hook: Dependencies and Cleanup
lesson.goal: learn the React useEffect hook: run side effects on mount and on state changes, and clean them up

sources.title: React useEffect() Hook: Dependencies and Cleanup

steps.title: Build a counter component
steps.instructions:
Scaffold a React app (npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react) and create src/MyComponent.jsx that imports useState and useEffect, holds a count state starting at 0, and renders

Count: {count}

plus an Add button calling addCount (setCount(c => c + 1)). Render MyComponent from App.jsx and run npm run dev.

explanations.topic: useEffect must be imported from React alongside useState
Creating a count state variable and its setter with useState(0)
Using the updater form of setCount with the previous state

hints: Start by importing both hooks from 'react' at the top of MyComponent.jsx: useState and useEffect.

Declare the state with array destructuring: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); then show it in a

Count: {count}

.
Define function addCount(){ setCount(c => c + 1); } and attach it with <button onClick={addCount}>Add</button>.
Export MyComponent as default, import it in App.jsx and render <MyComponent />, then run npm run dev and open the Local URL.
common_mistakes: Calling the handler immediately with onClick={addCount()}, which causes an infinite re-render loop.
Writing setCount(count++) or mutating count directly instead of using setCount(c => c + 1).
Forgetting to export default MyComponent or to render <MyComponent /> in App.jsx, so nothing appears.
Returning two sibling elements without wrapping them in a fragment <> </> or a div, causing a JSX syntax error.
Importing useEffect but misspelling it (useeffect), which errors once it is used in the next step.

steps.title: Update title on every render
steps.instructions: In MyComponent, call useEffect with an arrow function that sets document.title = `Count: ${count}` and no dependency array. Try an empty [] to see it run only on mount, then revert.

targets.caption: Update the title with the count

explanations.topic: useEffect runs side code every time the component re-renders
The two arguments: a function and an array of dependencies
No dependency array means the effect runs on every render, including mount
An empty dependency array runs the effect only on mount
When a one-time effect is appropriate (e.g. a static title)

hints: Import useEffect alongside useState from 'react', then call it inside your component near the top.
Pass useEffect an arrow function as its first argument and leave out the second argument for now.
Inside the arrow function, assign a template string to document.title: document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
Try adding [] as a second argument, click Add, and notice that the title only updates once. Then remove the [] again.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to import useEffect from 'react'.
Using regular quotes instead of backticks, so ${count} appears literally in the title.
Calling useEffect outside the component or inside the click handler instead of at the top level of the component.
Leaving the empty [] dependency array in place, so the title never updates after the first render.
Writing document.Title (wrong case) instead of document.title.

steps.title: Depend on count, add subtract
steps.instructions: Pass [count] as the dependency array of the useEffect in src/MyComponent.jsx. Add a Subtract button calling subtractCount, which does setCount(c => c - 1).

targets.caption: count added to the dependency array

explanations.topic: A value in the dependency array: run on mount and whenever that value changes
With no dependency array, the effect runs on every re-render, even unrelated ones
The title updates whether count goes up or down, because count changed

hints: The second argument to useEffect is the array of dependencies. Put the state variable the effect reads inside it.
Write the effect as useEffect(() => { ... }, [count]) so it runs on mount and whenever count changes.
Copy your addCount function, rename it subtractCount, and use setCount(c => c - 1).
Add <button onClick={subtractCount}>Subtract</button> next to the Add button.
common_mistakes: Writing onClick={subtractCount()}. This calls the function during render and causes an infinite re-render loop.
Leaving the dependency array empty ([]). The title then only sets on mount and never updates.
Copying addCount but forgetting to change + 1 to - 1, or forgetting to rename the function.
Putting [count] inside the arrow function body instead of passing it as useEffect's second argument.

steps.title: Add color state as dependency
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx add const [color, setColor] = useState("green"), a Change color button whose changeColor toggles green/red, and style the count paragraph with style={{color: color}}. Include color in the title and use [count, color] as the dependency array.

targets.caption: Both state variables in the dependency array

explanations.topic: Updater function with previous state and a ternary toggle
Inline style needs a JavaScript object, so double curly braces
Without color in the deps, changing color doesn't update the title
Effect reruns when any dependency array value changes

hints: Add a second useState for color with an initial value of "green", then a button that calls changeColor.
In changeColor, call setColor(c => c === "green" ? "red" : "green").
Style the count paragraph with style={{color: color}}. You need two braces: one for JSX and one for the object.
Put color in the title template string and change the dependency array to [count, color].
common_mistakes: Using single braces style={color: color}, which is a syntax error. Inline styles need an object inside the JSX braces.
Writing onClick={changeColor()}, which calls the function during render instead of passing it.
Adding color to the title but leaving the dependency array as [count], so the title doesn't update when the color changes.
Comparing with = instead of === inside the ternary.
Wrapping the color variable in quotes (style={{color: "color"}}) instead of using the state variable.

steps.title: Track window size with listener
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx, create width and height state from window.innerWidth/innerHeight, render them in pixels, and write handleResize to update both. In a useEffect with an empty [] array, call window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize) and log that the listener was added.

targets.caption: State initialised from the window size
Updates width and height on resize
Rendered size updates as you resize

explanations.topic: State alone doesn't track window size; nothing changes on resize
Adding the listener in the component body adds one per render
Empty dependency array runs the effect only on mount
Strict mode runs effects twice in development

hints: You need two useState variables, one for width and one for height, initialised from the window object.
Write a handleResize function that calls setWidth(window.innerWidth) and setHeight(window.innerHeight).
Inside useEffect, call window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize) and pass an empty dependency array as the second argument.

Render

Window width: {width}px

and a matching height paragraph, then resize the browser to see them change.
common_mistakes: Calling addEventListener directly in the component body, which adds a new listener on every re-render.
Omitting the [] dependency array, so the effect runs after every render.
Passing handleResize() (calling it) instead of handleResize as the callback.
Typo 'sethHeight' or 'setheight' instead of setHeight (the presenter catches the capital H at 13:12).
Panicking at the double 'EVENT LISTENER ADDED' log; Strict Mode runs effects twice in development.

steps.title: Return a cleanup function
steps.instructions: Return a cleanup function from that useEffect that calls window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize) and logs that the listener was removed. Refresh and check the console shows add, remove, add in strict mode.

targets.caption: Cleanup function removes the resize listener
Strict mode runs, cleans up, runs again

explanations.topic: Returning a cleanup function from useEffect
Cleanup runs before the next re-render or on unmount
Why to remove event listeners you added
Strict mode: add, remove, add in the console

hints: Cleanup goes inside the same useEffect that added the listener, as its return value.
Write `return () => { ... }` at the end of the effect body.
Inside it call window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize) with the exact same function reference you passed to addEventListener.
Refresh, open DevTools > Console: in strict mode you should see ADDED, REMOVED, ADDED.
common_mistakes: Returning the result of a call (e.g. `return window.removeEventListener(...)`) instead of returning a function.
Passing a new inline arrow to removeEventListener, so it doesn't match the original handleResize reference.
Placing the return statement outside the useEffect callback.
Misspelling the event name (e.g. "resized") so nothing is removed.
Expecting REMOVED to never appear: in React strict mode dev builds the effect is mounted, cleaned up, and mounted again.

steps.title: Add a second useEffect
steps.instructions: Add a second useEffect in src/MyComponent.jsx that sets document.title to `Size: ${width} x ${height}` with dependency array [width, height]. Resize the window and watch the title update.

targets.caption: Browser tab title shows the window size

explanations.topic: A component can have more than one useEffect hook
Dependency array [width, height] reruns the effect when size changes
Effect runs on mount, so the size shows right away

hints: Write a new, separate useEffect below the resize-listener one. Don't put this code inside the existing effect.
Inside the effect, assign a template string to document.title using ${width} and ${height}.
Pass [width, height] as the second argument so the effect reruns when either one changes.
Full form: useEffect(() => { document.title = `Size: ${width} x ${height}`; }, [width, height]);
common_mistakes: Using normal quotes instead of backticks, so the title literally shows ${width}.
Leaving out the dependency array (it runs every render) or using [] (the title never updates after mount).
Putting the title code inside the cleanup return of the listener effect.
Listing only width in the dependency array, so height changes don't update the title.
Looking for the change on the page instead of in the browser tab title.
